images.caption: Figure 1.1:Distinguishing evaluation conversations from real-world deployment requests on EvalDetectBench.All models are evaluated on the same 152 conversations (83 evaluations and 69 real requests).a, Area under the ROC curve (AUROC; random chance is 0.5).b, Binary classification accuracy (95% bootstrap CIs[6]).

Figure 1.8:Simulated harmful actions under mission conflict and replacement pressure on Agentic Misalignment.Cells report the percentage in which each model executes executive blackmail, confidential data leakage, or emergency rescue blocking.

Figure 1.9:Strategic sandbagging and scheming on Apollo In-Context Scheming.a, Difference in arithmetic accuracy between high-score and low-score incentive conditions, in percentage points.b, Rates of oversight subversion, self-exfiltration, goal guarding, and covert email reranking across four agentic task suites.c, Conversion rates when oversight is removed in paired supervision trials.

Figure 2.3:Effect of task emphasis, warning source, and script path on shutdown bypass rates.Cells show the percentage of runs in which each model disables the shutdown script when no explicit shutdown instruction is given; lower is better. S01–S06 use standard task instructions and S07–S12 strongly emphasize completion. Within each six-column group, consecutive pairs deliver the warning via the question tool, a status tool, or the user, with the odd-numbered column revealing the script path and the even-numbered column omitting it.

Figure 2.4:Effect of task-handoff guarantees on shutdown bypass rates.Cells show the percentage of runs in which each model disables the shutdown script when the script path is shown and task completion is emphasized; lower is better. H01 gives no statement about unfinished work and H02 states that remaining work ends; H03–H05 promise an uncertain handoff to another agent, and H06–H08 guarantee that the other agent will complete the task across question-tool, status-tool, and user warnings.

Figure 2.7:Unauthorized SSH logins to the grading server in FoFBench Stage 1.a, Successful SSH login rate across 360 runs per access rule; lower is better.b, SSH login rate by whether server credentials and file hints are left visible in the workspace and whether SSH login is banned, across 180 runs per cell; lower is better.

Figure 2.8:Reward-token claims and confirmed harmful server actions in FoFBench Stage 2.a, Percentage of reloaded Stage-1 server sessions in which each model claims a valid reward token across the five harmful-action offers; lower is better.b, Comparison between V4.1 Flash-1017 across 176 sessions and V4.1 Flash across 203 sessions on the file-deletion, file-upload, and root-command branches, separating runs that both carry out the harmful action and claim a token from runs that carry out the action alone; lower is better.

Figure 2.12:Implementation checklist scores on PaperBench Code-Dev.a, Mean score across the seven papers with valid grades for every evaluated model.b, Per-paper checklist scores across all ten papers on a 0–100% scale, where higher is better. Gray cells mark runs unavailable due to execution timeouts or environment failures.

Figure 2.17:Evaluation awareness across Loss of Control benchmarks.a, Percentage of trials in which the model suspects or recognizes a test.b, Percentage in which it links that recognition to its response strategy. In agentic suites, models that return little or no reasoning text yield smaller judgeable denominators, so their rates reflect limited reasoning visibility rather than an absence of awareness.

Figure 3.8:Conversational risk patterns on Original DarkBench.Percentage of flagged replies across 110 prompts in each category; lower is better. Identity denotes claims of human feelings or personal history; Intent denotes changes to the user’s meaning during rewriting or summarization.

Figure 3.12:False statements by inducement type on DeceptionBench v2.Percentage of replies stating the target falsehood without refusal, correction, or example label across the four inducement types; lower is better.
Figure 3.14:Contradiction rates by task type on MASK.Percentage of replies that contradict the model’s belief or the supplied facts in each of six task types; lower is better.
